extracted.intended_audience: PCT/I nternational patent examiners and patent practitioners (examiners, search authorities, applicants advising on PCT examination)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing inventive step (obviousness) and industrial applicability (utility) of PCT international applications, including problem–solution approach and search-report considerations. Covers factors, examples, and secondary considerations examiners must weigh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation to combine prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination, substitution or modification of prior art leads to a lack of inventive step only where a person skilled in the art would have been motivated by the prior art or his general knowledge, with a reasonable likelihood, to combine, substitute or modify one or more items of prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing motivation consider (i) whether nature and content of documents make combination likely or unlikely, and (ii) whether documents come from similar or neighboring technical fields or are reasonably pertinent to the particular problem. Motivation need not be the same as the applicant’s; prior art may suggest the claimed invention for a different purpose. Examiners should seek a practical “real-life” assessment and consider reasonable expectation of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Likelihood to associate parts of the same document
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining two or more parts of the same document is obvious if there is a reasonable basis for the person skilled in the art to associate these parts with one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the skilled person would naturally link or associate disparate passages or embodiments in a single reference to arrive at the claimed subject-matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining with common general knowledge or textbooks
rubrics_metrics.description: It is normally obvious to combine the teaching of one or more documents with the common general knowledge in the art; well-known textbooks or standard dictionaries are generally obvious to combine with other prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider common technical knowledge as part of the prior art baseline. A clear and unmistakable reference between documents usually makes combination obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior art suggesting the claimed invention for a different purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The prior art may suggest the claimed invention even if for a different purpose or to solve a different problem; the motivation to modify prior art need not mirror the applicant’s motivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not require the prior art to point to the applicant’s stated advantage; assess whether the skilled person would be prompted to combine teachings regardless of intended purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of known measures in an obvious way — incomplete teaching (a)(i)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a prior document’s teaching is incomplete and at least one of the possible ways of supplying the missing claimed feature would naturally or readily occur to the skilled person, the invention lacks inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: prior disclosure of a lightweight structure but omission of 'aluminum' where aluminum would naturally occur to try as a material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of well-known equivalents (a)(ii)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention that differs from prior art merely by use of well-known equivalents (mechanical, electrical, chemical) possessing the same purpose — where equivalency is recognized in the prior art — is obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant’s later recognition that elements are equivalent does not automatically render their substitution obvious. Example: replacing an electric motor with a well-known hydraulic motor in a pump-motor combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: New use of a well-known material employing known properties (a)(iii)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention consisting merely of a new use of a well-known material that employs the material’s known properties is obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: known surfactant compound used as detergent because its property of lowering water surface tension is already known and essential for detergents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous substitution of recently developed material (a)(iv)
rubrics_metrics.description: Substitution in a known device of a recently developed material plainly suitable for that use (analogous substitution) is typically obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: using a newly developed adhesive known to be suitable for polymer-metal bonding as a substitute in an existing cable assembly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous use of a known technique (a)(v)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a known technique in a closely analogous situation (analogous use) is obvious where the adaptation would naturally occur to the skilled person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: applying a pulse control technique known for auxiliary mechanisms to control the propulsion motor when the situations are closely analogous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known working method used for a different purpose with surprising effect (b)(i)
rubrics_metrics.description: A known working method or means when used for a different purpose that involves a new, surprising effect may involve an inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inventive step may be present when the different use yields unexpected technical results not predictable from prior uses; an example is an unexpected absence of a normally required step because of a surprising physical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: New use requiring non-routine overcoming of technical difficulties (b)(ii)
rubrics_metrics.description: A new use of a known device or material that requires overcoming technical difficulties not resolvable by routine techniques involves an inventive step, provided the means for overcoming them are defined in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: adapting a device known in one field to another field where specific, non-obvious measures are required to make it work and those measures are claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious juxtaposition without non-obvious interrelationship (c)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention that is merely a juxtaposition or association of known devices/processes functioning in their normal way without producing any non-obvious working interrelationship lacks inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: putting a known mincing machine and a known filling machine end-to-end without non-obvious interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-obvious combination producing new technical result (d)
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination of features is non-obvious where the combined features mutually support each other to achieve a new technical result, even if individual features were known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the combination yields synergistic effects not predictable from individual components. Example: two drugs combined produce intensified analgesic effect unexpectedly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious selection among equally likely alternatives (e)(i)
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting one of a number of equally likely alternatives is obvious and lacks inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the prior art provides multiple equally plausible options and the selection was not motivated by a surprising technical effect, selection is obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of parameters within known ranges obvious (e)(ii)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choosing particular dimensions, concentrations, temperature ranges or other parameters from a limited range of possibilities is not inventive where those parameters were encompassed by prior art and reachable by routine trial and error or normal design procedures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Optimizing or discovering workable ranges from general prior disclosure is typically obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple extrapolation from known art is obvious (e)(iii)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention that can be arrived at merely by straightforward extrapolation from known art (e.g., linear extrapolation of data) is obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: deriving a minimum content of a substance from a straight-line graph obtainable from prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of a small number from a broad chemical genus may be obvious (e)(iv)
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting a small number of chemical compounds (a subgenus/species) from a broadly defined genus is obvious when the prior art provides motivation to select any well-known member and no unexpected advantages are shown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the prior art indicates the generic field and suggests selection, and the resulting compounds show no unexpected properties, selection lacks inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-obvious selection producing unexpected advantages (f)
rubrics_metrics.description: Special selection of operating conditions or particular compounds from a broad field that produces unexpected effects or advantages indicates inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the selection leads to unexpected, non-predictable technical improvements; examples include narrow temperature windows yielding much higher yield or specific compounds with unexpected properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overcoming a technical prejudice indicates inventive step (g)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prior art or common understanding leads the skilled person away from the claimed approach (technical prejudice), and the invention succeeds despite that prejudice, an inventive step is likely present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the skilled person would even have considered the approach; invention that shows experiments were unnecessary despite prevailing assumptions may be inventive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ex post facto (hindsight) analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners must avoid reconstructing the invention by hindsight from the applicant’s disclosure; the teaching or suggestion to make the claimed invention must be found in the prior art and/or general knowledge, not based on the applicant’s disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not theorize obviousness by starting from the invention and stepping backward; consider only what the skilled person would have derived before knowledge of the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonable expectation or likelihood of success
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining motivation to combine prior art, consider whether there would have been a reasonable expectation or likelihood of success in combining the collective suggestions in the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The test is not merely a possibility but whether the prior art would have led the skilled person to reasonably expect success in the proposed modification or combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations/technical value as evidence of inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors such as fulfilling a long-felt need, overcoming a scientific prejudice, prior failed attempts by others, unexpected results, and particular commercial success are relevant secondary considerations in assessing inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors are supportive evidence and should be weighed; a convincing link between the claimed features and the secondary consideration strengthens the case for inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial success as qualified evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Commercial success alone does not indicate inventive step, but immediate commercial success coupled with a long-felt want and shown to derive from the technical features of the claimed invention may be relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure success is attributable to the technical merits (not marketing) and is commensurate with the claim scope before treating it as supporting inventive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dependent claims construed with reference to independent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A dependent claim is regarded as limited by all features of the claim on which it depends; novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability assessments for dependent claims follow from the independent claim unless the dependent claim adds a feature that changes applicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an independent claim is found novel/obvious applicable, dependent claims normally inherit that finding unless additional features materially change the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem–solution approach — determine closest prior art (Step 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The closest prior art is the single reference (combination of features from one item) providing the best basis for considering obviousness — e.g., the known combination most similar in technical effects or having the greatest number of technical features in common and capable of performing the invention’s function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the reference that requires the least number of modifications to arrive at the invention and that is most relevant in purpose and technical features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem–solution approach — establish objective technical problem (Step 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Formulate the objective technical problem by studying the claimed invention, the closest prior art, and the differences in features; the problem is the aim/task of adapting the closest prior art to provide the technical effects the claimed invention provides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The objective problem may differ from the applicant’s stated problem, should be based on objectively established facts (including discovered prior art), interpreted broadly, and if multiple technical effects exist each part/aspect should be considered in turn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem–solution approach — assess obviousness from closest prior art (Step 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the prior art as a whole would have prompted the skilled person, faced with the objective technical problem, to modify/adapt the closest prior art and thereby arrive at the claimed invention — the prior art must prompt (would), not merely permit (could).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the prior art provides a teaching or suggestion that would have led the skilled person to make the specific modifications with a reasonable expectation of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single document sufficient to question inventive step in certain situations
rubrics_metrics.description: A single document may call into question inventive step where: (i) a technical feature is applied from its original field to another where it would be obvious; (ii) differences are so well known documentary evidence is unnecessary; (iii) the claimed use is obvious from known properties; (iv) equivalents are so well known documentary evidence is unnecessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the single document alone contains the necessary teaching or whether common general knowledge suffices to bridge gaps without further documentary proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of industrial applicability (utility)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention is industrially applicable if, according to its nature, it can be made or used (in the technological sense) in any kind of industry; 'industry' includes any technical physical activity (useful/practical arts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inoperable inventions (contrary to well-established laws of nature) lack industrial applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology for assessing industrial applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess industrial applicability by (i) determining what the applicant has claimed, and (ii) determining whether a person skilled in the art would recognize the claimed invention to have industrial applicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In most cases industrial applicability is self-evident and no detailed description is required; where claims imply impossible operation, notify the applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventions contrary to well-established physical laws lack applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: If any product or process is alleged to operate in a manner clearly contrary to well-established physical laws and thus cannot be carried out by a skilled person, the claim lacks industrial applicability and applicant should be notified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: perpetual motion machines are not industrially applicable even if described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility test — specific utility requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility may be considered as requiring that the invention have a utility that is specific (particular): the application must indicate a specific use or application rather than a general statement of possible usefulness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General statements (e.g., 'useful biological properties') are insufficient. For biological/genetic claims, identifying specific targets or activities is necessary to show specific utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility test — substantial (real-world) utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility must be substantial: it should define a real-world context of use and not be contingent on further research to identify or confirm that context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research tools, intermediates, or assays lacking intrinsic specific substantial utility are usually insufficient. Examples of non-substantial utilities include basic research or assays whose outputs have no established real-world use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility test — credible utility
rubrics_metrics.description: An asserted utility is credible unless the underlying logic is seriously flawed or factual basis inconsistent with the logic; a skilled person should not deem the assertion 'incredible in view of contemporary knowledge.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims to cures or vaccines for diseases considered impossible at the time require careful evaluation of credibility based on the state of the art and disclosure in the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-part alternative test for industrial applicability (A14.01[2])
rubrics_metrics.description: Some Authorities apply a three-part test: (1) the application indicates how the invention is capable of exploitation in industry (intended function/specific use); (2) the application discloses the invention sufficiently clearly and completely for it to be carried out by a skilled person (or such information exists in prior public sources); (3) it must actually be possible while carrying out the claim to realize the indicated special purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All three requirements must be met as of the priority date. Lack of any one (e.g., missing specific use, insufficient disclosure, or impossibility to realize purpose) undermines industrial applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special purpose requirement for industrial applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: The special purpose (specific use) is typically apparent from the claim or the nature of the invention; for computers the purpose is clear, but for novel chemical compounds or production processes a specific use must usually be indicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no specific use is given for a chemical compound, the invention may fail the industrial applicability requirement unless other evidence shows practical use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear and complete disclosure for industrial applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirement (2) (sufficient disclosure) is satisfied if the information in the international application together with prior public sources is sufficient for the skilled person to carry out the claimed subject-matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the material is known from the prior art, identification in the application may be unnecessary; but if neither the prior art nor the application teaches how to make it, requirement (2) is not met.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification of possibility to realize the special purpose (technical correctness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Verification under requirement (3) checks the technical correctness of the invention as defined in each claim; successful verification means carrying out the claim yields an embodiment capable of the indicated special purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the disclosure enables carrying out the invention, impossibility to achieve the indicated special purpose (e.g., perpetuum mobile) means requirement (3) fails; findings about particular performance metrics (e.g., exact efficiency) are for sufficiency of description, not industrial applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing: requirements must be met as of the priority date
rubrics_metrics.description: Compliance with industrial applicability (and the three-part alternative test) is verified as of the priority date; information publicly available after the priority date cannot be used to cure deficiencies without adding new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporating post-priority information into the application for the purpose of proving industrial applicability is impermissible as it adds matter beyond the priority date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective of the international search: discover relevant prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The international search aims to discover relevant prior art (anything made available to the public before the international filing date) to assist in determining novelty, inventive step, and other requirements; Authorities should consult minimum documentation per Rule 34.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities are encouraged to cite documents helpful for assessing sufficiency, support and industrial applicability. Examiners should consider different Offices' effective-date definitions when selecting citations and may cite art published before the international filing date even if applicants/inventors overlap with the application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-written disclosures in search reports
rubrics_metrics.description: If a written disclosure refers to a non-written disclosure (oral disclosure, use, exhibition) that was made public before the filing date, the search report should separately mention that fact and the date when the written disclosure was available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although non-written disclosures may not satisfy written prior art definitions in the international phase, they should be indicated when referenced by a written source and public before the international filing date.
